questions.prompt: Walk through a POST to helios's /api/operations/commands from the first check to COMMIT. Name each gate in the order it runs and what a request that fails it gets back.

keyPoints.text: assertSameOrigin runs first: the request must be local and its Origin header must equal the configured application origin, or it is refused with ORIGIN_DENIED.
principalFromRequest is evaluated before the body is touched: the session cookie's HMAC is compared timing-safe, the expiry and persona are checked, and anything off is UNAUTHENTICATED (401).
readJson then insists on an application/json content type (415), caps the body at 16 KiB (413) and turns a parse failure into INVALID_JSON.
executeOperation parses the body against a strict discriminated union keyed on action, with a uuid commandId on every variant; a ZodError becomes 400 VALIDATION_FAILED with field paths.
Only then does idempotentCommand run its first statement, the role check: a persona whose role is not operator is refused as FORBIDDEN while no pool client has been borrowed yet.
transaction() checks out one client, issues BEGIN, runs the callback, and COMMITs; any throw issues ROLLBACK, and the client is always released.
Inside the transaction the order is: advisory lock on organization plus command id, receipt lookup, the operation's work on the same client, and the receipt insert last.

questions.prompt: Explain why helios keeps the schema parse and the operator check outside the database transaction but the receipt lookup inside it, behind a lock. For each, say what would change if it moved.

keyPoints.text: Parsing first means a malformed body never takes one of the pool's ten connections or a lock, and the receipt compares the parsed object rather than raw bytes.
keyPoints.quote: the compared input is the zod-parsed object from `executeOperation`, not the raw request body.

keyPoints.text: Checking the role before any lookup keeps a read-only caller from learning anything about stored commands: moved after the lookup, an existing command id would answer differently from a new one, and the caller would hold a connection and the lock while finding out.

The order is a choice of this envelope, not a law: the platform route calls requireOperator before it parses, so there a read-only persona with a malformed body gets the role refusal, while the operations route gives it the validation error.

The lookup sits behind pg_advisory_xact_lock on organization:command:id, so two concurrent sends of one command id queue; the second reads the first's committed receipt and replays instead of running the work again. The lock is transaction-scoped and needs no unlock.

Without that lock both would find no receipt and both run the work; the composite primary key would then fail one INSERT after its work, rolling it back and sending the client an error instead of the stored result.
Receipts are keyed by organization and command id and remember the actor, so a stored receipt from another operator or with different input is refused as IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT rather than handed back.
Putting the lookup, the work and the receipt in one transaction is what makes a receipt mean 'this committed'.
keyPoints.quote: ties the replay decision to durable success.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict this claim about helios's command envelope: "Any command can be retried blindly with the same commandId and body; the envelope guarantees it runs at most once and the client always sees the true outcome."

keyPoints.text: Only success leaves a receipt: the insert follows the work, so a domain refusal or a crash leaves nothing behind and the same command id later executes afresh against whatever state exists then.
That makes 'at most once' true for committed effects only; a failed attempt's outcome is not cached, so a retry can succeed where the first try was refused, or the reverse.
keyPoints.quote: A retry after a rollback is this case, not a replay.

keyPoints.text: A replay hands back the result stored at first commit, a snapshot that does not reflect anything that has changed since.
The atomicity covers only writes made through the client passed to the work; anything done on another connection is outside it.
keyPoints.quote: A function can throw after some independent writes have committed (for example, writes made through a different pool connection).

keyPoints.text: Which is why the test reads the tables after the failure instead of trusting the thrown error.
keyPoints.quote: The regression checks database state after the exception instead of assuming that a rejected promise proves rollback.

keyPoints.text: operation_commands keeps every receipt with only a created_at column and nothing in the code prunes it, so command ids are remembered forever and the table only grows.
The guarantee is per envelope, not per route: billing and platform commands reuse idempotentCommand, but the platform route's process_events and redrive_event actions return before reaching it.
